title: Red Sea shipping slows after Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, data shows
summary: Shipping through the Red Sea has slowed after a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, with vessel-tracking data and maritime analysts reporting fewer transits, wider rerouting around southern Africa, longer voyage times and rising insurance and operating costs. The disruption is affecting container and tanker schedules, adding delays to global supply chains and raising concerns over further escalation if attacks continue.
content:
Shipping through the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandeb strait has slowed in the days following a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, according to maritime data and industry analysts. Vessel-tracking platforms recorded a decline in transits along the shortest east-west route, while a notable number of commercial ships began rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope to avoid the area.

Analysts said the shift is increasing voyage lengths by several days for many carriers and pushing up fuel and operating costs. War risk insurance premiums for ships transiting the region have risen, prompting some owners to delay sailings or choose longer, more expensive routes to mitigate perceived security risks.

Both container lines and oil tankers have been affected. Container schedules showed a growing number of missed port calls and cascading delays at major hubs, while tankers were reported to be diverting away from the Red Sea corridor, creating timing uncertainty for crude and fuel deliveries to Europe and Asia.

The slowdown follows attacks by Houthi forces in Yemen that targeted facilities in Saudi Arabia, an escalation that has prompted heightened caution across the shipping industry. Maritime analytics firms and trading desks monitoring vessel movements said the patterns were consistent with a temporary but significant reduction in traffic through the narrow chokepoint.

Governments and naval forces in the region have reiterated calls for the protection of commercial shipping lanes, and some naval escorts have been increased for high-value or vulnerable cargoes. Shipping associations urged a coordinated response to secure the corridor and to limit disruptions to global trade while also warning of the economic impact if the security situation persists.

Market watchers said the immediate effect on freight rates and commodity prices has been mixed, reflecting both the rerouting costs and wider market factors. Industry participants noted that the longer-term consequences will depend on whether further attacks occur and how quickly insurers and ship operators adjust routing and coverage decisions.

Shipping companies and logistics providers are now assessing the cost and time impacts on contracts and supply chains, with some firms issuing customer notices about expected delays. The broader trade community is watching closely for signs of either de-escalation or more sustained interruption to Red Sea transits, which play a key role in connecting Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal.
